claims.text: Step 3 of system-design-method.md is the high-level design; its output is one diagram of the main parts and the path of each key operation through it; step 1's output includes the key operations; step 4 details one to three parts.
The method's refund example looks back at the stage-3 flow and decides nothing new; the estimate concluded load does not shape refunds (about 0.03 requests per second).

The method's refund diagram has seven parts: customer app or web, entry point, DonHang.Api (donhang: orders, outbox_messages), RabbitMQ, DonHang.Payments (donhang_payments: payments), payment gateway, DonHang.Notifications (donhang_notifications).

Ranked refund drivers (step 1): YC-7 (answered within 2 seconds even when the gateway fails), YC-9 (never refund twice), the gateway API key and money rows as most sensitive. The entry point is unnamed in the method's diagram.

The outbox and async step exist because YC-7 needs an answer while the gateway fails; RabbitMQ carries that step because Payments is a separate service (no 2PC); Payments is split off so only it holds the gateway key.
The refund diagram contains no cache; at about 0.03 refund requests per second no number calls for one.

claims.text: Each store has one owner (module or service); no service writes another's database. The API, owner of orders, sets cancelled on payment.refunded, back to paid on payment.refund-failed, and writes order.refunded / order.refund-failed to its outbox.

claims.text: Paths: submit = refunding + outbox in one transaction, 202 Accepted; send = relay (OutboxRelay, inside each service) to RabbitMQ, Payments pending row, job retries the gateway; result = Payments' own outbox, API, email; staff = GET /api/v1/refunds?status=failed.

claims.text: data-ownership.md: orders by Ordering in donhang; payments/refunds by Payments in donhang_payments; the old payments table in donhang is a copy nobody updates, and on mismatch trust donhang_payments (so answering from it gives stale data); emails by Notifications.
Ordering is a module inside DonHang.Api; Notifications and Payments are separate services each owning a database.

claims.text: Trade-offs of first drawings: normal path only misses failure waits; parts up front add operating cost with no driver; fewest parts walked with failures catches missing arrows and two-writer stores; detailing every part spends time where no driver makes it hard.
The method does not detail the staff failed list: no driver makes it hard, it is only a read query.
refund-design.md risk R1: if the gateway reports results later by calling back into the system, step 6 (Payments records the gateway's confirmation) must change.
Method failure table: DonHang.Notifications (1 instance) down: submitting runs; the order is still cancelled and only the email waits.
refund-design.md rejects calling the gateway inside the customer's request: when the gateway fails or is slow the customer waits and gets an error and the request is not recorded, contrary to YC-7.

A high-level design shows parts, owners and paths, not classes or columns; each extra part is more to run, fail and keep current, so it belongs only where a driver or estimate calls for it (a cache for read load, a queue for a failure to survive).
In the method's diagram (lines 96-106) the entry point has a single arrow, to DonHang.Api; no arrow from the entry point reaches DonHang.Payments, although the staff path (lines 117-118) goes there.

RabbitMQ carries the refund messages between the services (order.refund-requested, payment.refunded, payment.refund-failed, order.refunded, order.refund-failed); no version-specific behaviour is described.
